title: Feelings in depth
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: ser or estar with an adjective is not permanent against temporary — it CHANGES THE WORD'S MEANING. es aburrido is boring and está aburrido is bored; es rico is wealthy and está rico is delicious; es listo is clever and está listo is ready (L2-M2's row already says so). The slogan dies on está muerto, which is as permanent as anything gets.
A feeling you are IN takes estar, and the adjective agrees with the person feeling it: estoy preocupado / estoy preocupada, estamos hartos. The verb never changes the word; only the ending moves.

gustar is not a one-off, it is a CLASS: encantar, molestar, importar, faltar and doler (L2-M8's) all run the same way. The thing is the SUBJECT and the person is an indirect object, so the verb follows the thing: me encanta el libro, me encantan los libros.

encantar already means love, so it takes no muy and no mucho. me encanta mucho is not a stronger like, it is a learner's sentence. For the smaller feeling, gustar with mucho is what a speaker reaches for.

Spanish keeps some feelings as NOUNS and hands them to tener: tengo miedo, tengo ganas de, tengo vergüenza, tengo hambre. They are things you HAVE, so nothing agrees with you and neither ser nor estar appears.
me da + noun is the same backwards shape with dar (L2-M1's) as the verb — the thing gives the feeling to me: me da pena, me da igual, me da miedo. What follows da is a noun, never an adjective.

sentences.display: Estoy aburrido, pero no soy aburrido.
sentences.cue: I'm bored, but I'm not boring.
sentences.literal: I-am bored, but not I-am boring.

words.note: One word, two meanings, and the verb picks: es aburrido is boring, está aburrido is bored. Say it of a person with ser and you have called them dull.

sentences.trap: English has two words, bored and boring. Spanish has one, and the verb in front of it is what tells them apart.

mistake.display: Soy aburrido, pero no soy aburrido.
mistake.why: Both halves now say boring, so the sentence contradicts nothing. The state needs estar: estoy aburrido.

sentences.usage: A joke you can make about a slow afternoon. First person throughout; no address is chosen.
sentences.mnemonic: ser says what you ARE; estar says how you are RIGHT NOW.

sentences.display: Este café está rico. Mi jefe es rico.
sentences.cue: This coffee is delicious. My boss is rich.
sentences.literal: This coffee is delicious. My boss is rich.

words.note: es rico is wealthy; está rico is delicious, and it is what people say about food. ¡Qué rico! at a table is about the meal, never about the cook.

sentences.trap: Nothing in the word rico tells you which meaning is meant. está or es does, every time.
sentences.sound: RI-co, stressed on the first syllable, and the r is a single tap, not the rolled one that starts a word.
sentences.usage: The first half is what you say over a meal; the second is gossip. Neutral in both, and no second person appears.

sentences.display: Me encanta la música, y me encantan los libros.
sentences.cue: I love music, and I love books.
sentences.literal: To-me it-enchants the music, and to-me they-enchant the books.

words.note: The gustar shape one step up: me encanta la música, me encantan los libros. The verb follows the thing, not me, and it already means love, so no muy.

sentences.trap: The verb changes because the BOOKS are plural, not because I am. me is never the subject of these verbs.

mistake.why: That makes me the subject and says roughly I enchant myself. The books do the enchanting: me encantan los libros.

sentences.usage: Ordinary enthusiasm, said about anything from food to a city. First person; no address chosen.

sentences.display: Me molesta el ruido de la calle.
sentences.cue: The noise from the street bothers me.
sentences.literal: To-me it-bothers the noise of the street.

words.note: Same shape as me gusta, opposite feeling: the noise is the subject. One thing takes me molesta, more than one takes me molestan.
Noise of any kind — traffic, a party, a neighbour. hacer ruido is what a noisy thing does, and it is masculine: el ruido.

sentences.trap: English puts the noise first and me last; Spanish puts me first and the noise last, and the noise is still the subject.
sentences.usage: A complaint to a friend, or to a landlord. Neutral enough for both, and it names no one.

sentences.display: No me importa. Me da igual.
sentences.cue: I don't mind. It's all the same to me.
sentences.literal: Not to-me it-matters. To-me it-gives equal.

words.note: Literally it matters to me, so the thing is the subject. No me importa is I don't mind — it is not the cold English I don't care.

words.cue: it's all the same to me
words.note: Three words, one surface. Said warmly it opens the choice to you; said flat it says you have stopped caring, so tone is what decides.

sentences.trap: Neither half is the English I don't care. Both are polite ways of handing the choice to the other person.

mistake.why: That says I don't matter. The thing is the subject and me is the person it matters to: no me importa.

sentences.usage: The answer when someone asks which one you want and you truly have no preference. Warm tone required.

sentences.display: Me da pena tu hermano. No está tranquilo.
sentences.cue: I feel sorry for your brother. He isn't at ease.
sentences.literal: To-me it-gives pity your brother. Not he-is calm.

words.note: The thing gives me pena. It covers pity and a mild sadness at once — me da pena tu hermano is I feel for him, not I look down on him.
Calm, unhurried, at ease. Alone, ¡Tranquilo! is what you say to someone who is worrying — nearer to it's fine than to be quiet.

sentences.trap: What follows da is a noun — pena. Spanish will not take an adjective there, so me da triste is not a sentence.
sentences.usage: Said about someone you both know. tu chooses the informal address, so this is a friend, not a counter clerk.

sentences.display: Tengo miedo de hablar con el jefe.
sentences.cue: I'm afraid of talking to the boss.
sentences.literal: I-have fear of to-speak with the boss.

words.note: Fear is a noun you HAVE. soy miedoso would say you are a fearful person by nature, which is a claim about your character, not your evening.

sentences.trap: Fear is HAD, not been. And what you are afraid of arrives with de plus an infinitive, never with a que clause here.

mistake.display: Soy miedoso de hablar con el jefe.
mistake.why: miedoso describes your character — a timid person. The evening's fear is tengo miedo.

sentences.usage: An admission to a friend or a colleague. First person, and el jefe keeps it work-shaped.

sentences.display: Tengo ganas de ver a mis amigos.
sentences.cue: I feel like seeing my friends.
sentences.literal: I-have urges of to-see to my friends.

words.note: The everyday I feel like doing something, and de is not optional: tengo ganas de ver a mis amigos. A noun after it wants the de too.

sentences.trap: ganas is a noun and it is plural in the frame — tengo ganas, never tengo gana. The de is fixed too.
sentences.usage: How a plan gets floated. The a before mis amigos is the personal a, because they are people.
sentences.mnemonic: tener + noun for a feeling: miedo, ganas, hambre, sed.

sentences.display: Estoy preocupado, pero estoy orgulloso de mi hermana.
sentences.cue: I'm worried, but I'm proud of my sister.
sentences.literal: I-am worried, but I-am proud of my sister.

words.note: Worried, and it takes estar because it is a state you are in. What the worry is about arrives with por: preocupado por mi madre.
Proud, and proud OF takes de: orgulloso de mi hermana. With ser it drifts towards arrogant, so estar is the one you want about a feeling.

sentences.trap: Both adjectives agree with the SPEAKER, not with the sister. A woman saying this writes preocupada and orgullosa.
sentences.usage: Said about family, plainly. First person; the sister is talked about, not addressed.

sentences.display: Mi padre está enfadado. Estoy harto.
sentences.cue: My father is angry. I've had enough.
sentences.literal: My father is angry. I-am fed-up.

words.note: Angry, in Spain; much of Latin America says enojado for the same feeling. Both take estar — it is a state, not a character.
Fed up, had enough. estar harto de is the full frame: estoy harto de esperar. Blunt, but not rude.

sentences.trap: Both are states, so both take estar. es enfadado would claim anger is what your father is made of.
sentences.usage: A complaint between friends. Blunt but not rude; harto is the word a Spaniard reaches for when patience is gone.
